title: Demographic transition is splitting the world between population ageing and continued growth, reshaping care, work, migration, and state capacity
source_unit: UN DESA Population Division, World Population Prospects 2024: Summary of Results
geography: 237 countries or areas, with global, regional, and national demographic estimates and projections to 2100

denominator.unit: countries or areas covered by World Population Prospects 2024 estimates and projections

population_peak.unit: global population projected around the mid-2080s

population_2100.unit: global population projected by the end of the century, approximately

peak_probability.unit: percent estimated probability that global population peaks within the current century

observations.method: UN DESA demographic estimates and probabilistic projections based on fertility, mortality, migration, age, and sex trends, with country and regional projections through 2100.
observations.uncertainty: Projections are scenario-dependent and sensitive to future fertility, mortality, migration, conflict, policy, and data revisions. A global peak does not imply simultaneous decline or reduced pressure in every country or region.
observations.subgroup: Countries and areas with already-peaked, growing, or rapidly growing populations, plus populations differentiated by age, sex, fertility, mortality, and migration.
observations.counterinterpretation: Lower aggregate population growth may reduce some environmental pressures but does not remove the need to reduce per-person impact; population decline can also coexist with high consumption, fiscal strain, or uneven access to care and housing.

denominator.unit: countries or areas in the UN demographic estimate and fertility comparison frame

global_fertility_2024.unit: live births per woman globally in 2024

global_fertility_1990.unit: live births per woman globally around 1990

below_replacement_countries.unit: share of countries and areas with fertility below 2.1 live births per woman

ultra_low_fertility.unit: share of countries and areas with fertility below 1.4 live births per woman

observations.method: UN DESA comparison of historical and current fertility estimates, replacement-level classifications, and population-peak trajectories.
observations.uncertainty: Replacement fertility is a long-run demographic benchmark, not a social target or measure of individual wellbeing. Country averages conceal desired family size, access to care and contraception, economic constraints, and differences in migration.
observations.subgroup: Countries with ultra-low fertility and peaked populations, countries with high fertility and continued growth, women and families at different ages, and populations affected by education, health, care, and labour-market conditions.
observations.counterinterpretation: Fertility decline can reflect expanded choice and education as well as affordability, housing, care, insecurity, or postponed partnership; demographic projections should not be converted into pronatalist or anti-migration conclusions without examining agency and constraints.

observations.period: 1995-2054; life expectancy, ageing, and population structure

denominator.unit: global population mortality, longevity, and age-structure projection frame

life_expectancy_2024.unit: years of global life expectancy at birth in 2024

life_expectancy_1995.unit: years of global life expectancy at birth around 1995, implied by an 8.4-year increase

older_death_share_2050s.unit: more than percent of global deaths projected to occur at age 80 or higher by the late 2050s

older_than_children.value: by the late 2070s, persons aged 65 or older are projected to outnumber children under 18 globally

observations.method: UN DESA mortality, life-expectancy, and age-structure estimates and projections, including post-pandemic recovery in global longevity.
observations.uncertainty: Age thresholds are administrative and culturally variable; life expectancy is not healthy life expectancy, care need, or work capacity. Aggregate ageing does not reveal how longevity, disability, wealth, or family support are distributed.
observations.subgroup: Older people, children, working-age populations, caregivers, health and social-protection systems, labour markets, and countries at different stages of demographic transition.
observations.counterinterpretation: Longer lives can support work, learning, care, and social participation when health, accessibility, income, and institutions improve; ageing is not synonymous with dependency or fiscal collapse.

boundary: This record adds a demographic-transition-to-care, work, migration, place, and state-capacity route. It is not individual fertility or family-preference data, does not establish causal effects of demographic change on household behavior or political action, and does not treat population projections as normative targets.

The hash is a source-URL fingerprint for the report landing page.
